nameStory: The Arrowhead Borer gets its name from the distinctive arrow-shaped markings on its wing covers, which look like Native American arrowheads pointing toward the beetle's head. This longhorn beetle is also called the Pine Bark Runner, reflecting its habit of scurrying quickly across pine bark when disturbed.
description: The Arrowhead Borer is a medium-sized longhorn beetle with a sleek, elongated body typical of its family. Adults are brownish-black with striking white or cream-colored arrow-shaped markings on their wing covers that give them their common name. Like other longhorn beetles, they have notably long antennae that can be as long as their body. They typically measure about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long.

idTips.label: Arrow markings
idTips.description: Look for distinctive white or cream arrow-shaped marks on dark wing covers that point toward the beetle's head - these are the most reliable identifying feature

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Notice the antennae that extend nearly as long as the beetle's body, a classic longhorn beetle trait that you can see even when the beetle is moving

idTips.label: Body color
idTips.description: The base color is dark brownish-black with a somewhat matte finish, not shiny like some other beetles

idTips.label: Size and shape
idTips.description: About the length of your thumbnail with a narrow, cylindrical body that feels smooth and hard to the touch if handled gently

idTips.label: Movement pattern
idTips.description: When disturbed, they run quickly across bark surfaces rather than immediately flying away, earning them the nickname 'bark runner'

habitat: Look for Arrowhead Borers in coniferous forests throughout New England, especially areas dominated by pine, spruce, and fir trees. They're most commonly found on dead or dying conifers where the larvae develop under the bark. You'll spot adults crawling on tree trunks, stumps, and recently cut logs in both lowland and montane forests.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm. Look for them sunning themselves on tree trunks during warm afternoons.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most visible crawling on bark and seeking mates. This is the best time to spot their distinctive arrow markings.
seasonality.fall: Adult activity continues into early fall, though they become less active as temperatures drop. Late-season adults may be preparing to overwinter.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter hidden in bark crevices or under loose bark, rarely visible unless you carefully examine sheltered spots on dead trees.

funFact: The larvae of Arrowhead Borers create elaborate zigzag galleries under pine bark that look like abstract art - these intricate tunnels can persist for years after the beetle has emerged, creating a hidden record of their childhood beneath the bark!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with its close relative, the Rustic Borer, which also lives on conifers. The key difference is the arrow pattern - Rustic Borers have more irregular white markings that don't form clear arrowhead shapes. Remember: 'Arrows for Arrowhead' - if you see distinct arrow shapes, you've found the right beetle.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'borer' alarm you - while the larvae do tunnel under bark, Arrowhead Borers typically only attack trees that are already dead, dying, or severely stressed. They're actually part of nature's cleanup crew, helping decompose dead wood rather than harming healthy trees.
compareHints: Compared to its closest relative, the Rustic Borer, the Arrowhead Borer has much more organized and distinct arrow-shaped white markings rather than the Rustic Borer's scattered, irregular white patches. Both species prefer conifers, but Arrowhead Borers have cleaner, more geometric patterns that make identification easier once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: The rustic borer differs from its close relative the arrowhead borer by having gray bands instead of distinct arrow-shaped white markings.
